newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF says shares BOJ monetary stance.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF says shares BOJ monetary stance.

text.p: Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday that the ministry's stance on monetary policy matched the views of the Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor.
"Our monetary policy follows the basic stance that the BOJ governor has outlined in his news conferences," Mitsuzuka said.
BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita has said that Japan's monetary policy emphasises strengthening the basis for Japan's economic recovery.

Mitsuzuka said monetary policy forms one of the pillars of a country's economic policy. A country may raise interest rates to prevent inflation and may lower rates for the sake of stable economic growth, he said.
Japan has been keeping its key interest rates at record lows to help tackle economic woes arising from the bursting of the nation's economic bubble, he said.
"Japan has been doing its best on economic policy and may have to ask those depending on interest rate income for a living to bear something of a burden for a while," he said.
On currencies, Mitsuzuka said Japan will deal with movements in foreign exchange markets as agreed in the Group of Seven (G7) meeting of finance ministers and central bankers in Berlin in February.
The G7 nations agreed at that time that major misalignments in currencies noted at their meeting in April 1995 had been corrected. They also called for stability in the foreign exchange markets.
"The correction started in 1995 and is now on a generally good trend," Mitsuzuka said.

"An excessively weak as well as an excessively strong yen is not favourable. In the February (G7) agreement, we said that we will watch foreign exchange movements carefully and act appropriately. We will deal with currencies in line with this agreement," he said.

Asked whether Japan would be able to achieve its official forecast of 2.5 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1997, he said that the 2.5 percent target will definitely be achieved and may even be exceeded slightly.
Mitsuzuka said that an economic recovery based on private sector demand was gradually falling into place in Japan and that he did not think Japan's trade surplus would expand drastically.
